title: Scope and lifetime
goal: Say where each variable's name can be used (file scope, block scope, hiding) and how long it lives (automatic versus static storage duration), and trace what-does-it-print programs that mix globals, static locals and shadowed names.

topics.title: Scope: where a name can be used
topics.examNote: Exam tracing questions often reuse one name (`x`, `total`, `i`) at several levels. For every use of the name, ask: *which declaration is the nearest one above me, in my block or a block around me?* That is the variable being used.

blocks.text:
Today is about two questions you must be able to answer for every variable in a program:

1. **Scope**: in which part of the program can you use the *name*?
2. **Lifetime**: during which part of the *run* does the variable exist and hold a value?

This lesson is scope. The next lesson is lifetime.

### Two kinds of scope you will use all the time

The **scope** of a name (an *identifier*) is the region of the program text where the name can be used.

- **File scope**: the name is declared *outside* every function. It can be used from the line where it is declared to the end of the file. A variable with file scope is usually called a **global variable**.
- **Block scope**: the name is declared *inside* a block (a pair of braces `{ }`), or it is a function parameter. It can be used from its declaration to the closing `}` of that block. A variable with block scope is usually called a **local variable**.

A `for` loop counts as a block too: in `for (int i = 0; ...)`, the `i` exists only inside the loop.

Here is the notebook's `scope.c`, with a comment on each declaration:

blocks.caption: scope.c (from the notebook, comments added)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o scope scope.c
$ ./scope
main: j = 0
	func: i = 101, j = 1
		for loop, i = 0, j = 2
		for loop, i = 1, j = 2
	func: i = 101, j = 1
main: j = 0

blocks.text:
`\t` in a `printf` string is a **tab** character; the notebook uses it to indent the lines printed inside `f`.

Notice **where** each name was declared:

- `j`, `f`, `k` and `main` all have file scope, but each starts at its own line. `k` is declared *after* `f`, so `f` cannot use `k`.
- `main` never sees a local `j`, so it uses the global `j`. A global variable starts at 0 (more on why in the next lesson), so `main` prints 0 both times: `f` changed only its own `j`.

### Using a name before (or after) its scope is a compile error

If `f` tries to use `k`, gcc stops, even though `k` is declared later in the same file:

blocks.caption: kscope.c: k is used before its declaration

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o kscope kscope.c
kscope.c: In function 'f':
kscope.c:4:5: error: 'k' undeclared (first use in this function)
    4 |     k = k + 1;
      |     ^
kscope.c:4:5: note: each undeclared identifier is reported only once for each function it appears in

blocks.text: The same thing happens when you use a loop variable after its loop has ended:

blocks.caption: loopi.c: i only exists inside the loop

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o loopi loopi.c
loopi.c: In function 'main':
loopi.c:7:27: error: 'i' undeclared (first use in this function)
    7 |     printf("after: %d\n", i);
      |                           ^
loopi.c:7:27: note: each undeclared identifier is reported only once for each function it appears in

blocks.text: If you need the value after the loop, declare the variable *before* the loop (`int i;` then `for (i = 0; ...)`).

### Hiding (shadowing)

Blocks sit inside other blocks, so scopes are **nested**. C allows you to declare the same name again in an inner scope. Inside the inner scope, the *inner* declaration wins and the outer one is **hidden** (another common word for this is *shadowed*). When the inner block ends, the outer name is visible again. It is legal, but it is confusing, so avoid it in your own code. Exams use it on purpose.

blocks.caption: shadow.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o shadow shadow.c
$ ./shadow
A: x = 1
B: x = 2
C: x = 3
D: x = 2

blocks.text:
Line by line:

- `A`: `main` has no `x` of its own yet (its `x` is declared on the next line), so this is the global `x`, 1.
- `B`: `main`'s `x` now hides the global one.
- `C`: inside the inner block, the innermost `x` (3) wins.
- `D`: the inner block has ended and its `x` is gone, so we are back to `main`'s `x`, still 2. Changing an inner `x` never changes an outer one: they are *different variables* that happen to share a name.

gcc does not warn about hiding with `-Wall`. Compile shadow.c with an extra flag: `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wshadow -o shadow shadow.c`. You get `warning: declaration of 'x' shadows a global declaration` and `... shadows a previous local`. Handy when a program prints a value you did not expect.

blocks.q: In scope.c, the parameter `i` of `f` is 101 before the loop. What is it after the loop, and why?
blocks.a: Still 101. The loop declares a *new* `i` that hides the parameter only inside the loop. The loop changes its own `i` (0, then 1); the parameter is never touched.

blocks.text:
### A third kind: function prototype scope

The parameter names in a prototype (a declaration without a body) have **function prototype scope**: they exist only up to the end of that prototype. It rarely matters, with one exception the notebook points out: a name must be declared before it is used, even inside the parameter list. So `void g(int n, int a[n]);` is correct, but `void g(int a[n], int n);` is an error (`'n' undeclared`), because `n` is used before it comes into scope. (There is a fourth kind, *function scope*, used only for labels; CISC220 does not use it.)

### Key points

- **Scope** = where in the program text a name can be used.
- **File scope** (global): declared outside all functions; usable from its line to the end of the file.
- **Block scope** (local): declared inside `{ }` or as a parameter; usable from its line to the block's `}`. A `for (int i ...)` variable lives only in the loop.
- Using a name outside its scope is a compile error: `'k' undeclared`.
- An inner declaration **hides** (shadows) an outer one with the same name until the inner block ends. They are different variables.
- To find which variable a use refers to: look for the nearest declaration *above* it, in its own block or an enclosing block, then at file scope.

topics.title: Lifetime: automatic and static storage duration
topics.examNote: The classic trace: a function with an ordinary local and a `static` local, called several times. The ordinary one restarts on every call; the `static` one is initialized once and remembers. Write a small table of each variable's value after each call.

blocks.text:
### Lifetime and storage duration

The **lifetime** of a variable is the part of the run during which it exists in memory and holds a value. C decides the lifetime from the variable's **storage duration**. The notebook lists four kinds: *automatic*, *static*, *allocated* (Day 18, `malloc`) and *thread* (not in CISC220). Today: the first two.

### Automatic storage duration: ordinary local variables

A variable declared inside a block (without the word `static`), and every function parameter, has **automatic** storage duration:

- its memory is set aside when the program **enters** its block,
- and it is released when the program **leaves** the block, by any means (reaching its `}` or a `return`).

So a function's locals are created fresh on *every* call and destroyed when the call returns. A variable declared inside a loop body is created and destroyed on *every iteration*.

Automatic variables are **not** initialized for you. Without `= value`, the starting value is *indeterminate* (whatever bits were in that memory). You met this on Day 4 with the notebook's `sum_of.c` bug: `unsigned long sum;` and then `sum += i`. Reading such a variable is a bug, and the output can change from run to run or computer to computer, so no fixed output can be predicted.

### Static storage duration

Two kinds of variables have **static** storage duration:

1. every variable with **file scope** (globals), and
2. every variable declared with the keyword **`static`**, including one declared *inside* a function.

A static-duration variable lives for the **whole run** of the program. It is initialized **exactly once**, before `main` starts. And if you do not give it a starting value, C sets it to zero: `0` for integers, `0.0` for `double` (and a *null pointer* for pointers, which you will meet on Day 11).

blocks.caption: defaults.c: static-duration variables start at zero

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o defaults defaults.c
$ ./defaults
g = 0, d = 0.000000, s = 0

blocks.text:
### A `static` local keeps its value between calls

Compare an ordinary local with a `static` local in the same function:

blocks.caption: visit.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o visit visit.c
$ ./visit
a = 1, s = 1
a = 1, s = 2
a = 1, s = 3

blocks.text:
- `a` is automatic: every call makes a new `a`, sets it to 0, adds 1, prints 1, and the `a` dies at the `}`.
- `s` is static: there is only **one** `s`. The line `static int s = 0;` is *not* run on each call; it is an initialization done once before the program starts. Each call adds 1 to the same `s`, so it remembers 1, 2, 3.

The **scope** of `s` is still only the body of `visit`: no other function can use the name `s`. Static changes the *lifetime*, not the scope. That is the point: the value is remembered, but only `visit` can touch it.

The notebook's example is a counter whose value can be read (with `count(0)`) or increased:

blocks.caption: counter.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o counter counter.c
$ ./counter
current count = 0
increment, current count = 1
increment, current count = 2
increment, current count = 3
current count = 3

blocks.q: In counter.c, the first call is `count(0)`. Why does it print 0, and why does the last call `count(0)` print 3?
blocks.a: `value` is a static local, initialized to 0 once. `count(0)` does not add anything, so it returns the current value: 0 at the start. Three `count(1)` calls add 1 each to the *same* `value`, so it is 3, and the final `count(0)` returns that 3.

blocks.text: ### Inside a loop body: new every iteration, unless static

blocks.caption: loopt.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o loopt loopt.c
$ ./loopt
10 11 12 
10 11 13

blocks.text: First loop: a new `t` is made with 10 on each pass, so we print 10 + 0, 10 + 1, 10 + 2. Second loop: one `t`, set to 10 once; it becomes 10, then 11, then 13.

A `static` variable's initializer must be a **constant** that the compiler can work out, because it is applied before the program runs. `static int value = start;` (with `start` a parameter) is a compile error:

```
nonconst.c:4:24: error: initializer element is not constant
```

### `static` at file scope, and a common bug

Writing `static` in front of a **file scope** variable (or function) does not change its lifetime (it already lives for the whole run). It changes its **linkage**: the name is visible only inside this one source file, so another `.c` file linked into the same program cannot use it. The notebook compares it to a `private static` field in Java. (Linkage between several files comes up again later in the course.)

The notebook's `sum_of2_fails.c` shows the danger of keeping a result in a long-lived variable:

blocks.caption: sum_of2_fails.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o sum_of2_fails sum_of2_fails.c
$ ./sum_of2_fails
sum_of(10) = 55
sum_of(10) = 110

blocks.text: The second call starts from the 55 that the first call left in `sum`, so it prints 110. The notebook's advice: do not use a static variable here at all. Use a local running total and **return** it, and pass the value to print as a parameter:

blocks.caption: sum_fixed.c: the fix the notebook suggests

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o sum_fixed sum_fixed.c
$ ./sum_fixed
sum_of(10) = 55
sum_of(10) = 55

blocks.q: If static locals are so handy, why does the notebook say functions that remember things between calls are uncommon?
blocks.a: A function whose result depends on hidden history is hard to test and easy to misuse: the same call can give different answers (like `sum_of(10)` giving 110). Parameters and return values make the data flow visible. Use a static local only when remembering *is* the job (a counter, an ID generator). The Standard Library function `strtok` is a famous example.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- **Lifetime** = when the variable exists during the run; it comes from the **storage duration**.
- **Automatic** (ordinary locals and parameters): created when the block is entered, destroyed when it is left; created again on every call and every loop iteration. Not initialized: always give a starting value.
- **Static** (all globals, and anything declared `static`): one copy for the whole run, initialized **once** before `main`, to 0 if you give no value.
- A `static` local keeps its value between calls but can only be *used* inside its function (static changes lifetime, not scope). Its initializer must be a constant.
- `static` on a file scope name makes it private to that file (internal linkage).
- Prefer locals + `return` over results kept in globals or statics.

topics.title: When a lifetime ends too soon, and tracing exam programs
topics.examNote: April 2022 Q5(a) asks whether data a function saved from one of its own local variables is still valid after the function returns, and wants the reason: the local's lifetime ended. Fall 2014 Q3 asks for a program that remembers the previous number to report a difference; a `static` local (or a variable in `main`) is how you remember.

blocks.text:
### Returning a local array: the object is dead

On Day 5 you learned that an array name used as a value turns into the **address** of its first element, and that a function cannot return an array. A tempting trick is to return that address. The notebook shows why it fails. (`int *` means *pointer to `int`*, an address of an `int`, the same type you saw for array parameters on Day 5. Pointers get full lessons on Days 11 and 12.)

blocks.caption: badarray.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o badarray badarray.c
badarray.c: In function 'intarray':
badarray.c:8:12: warning: function returns address of local variable [-Wreturn-local-addr]
    8 |     return arr;
      |            ^~~
$ ./badarray
Segmentation fault

blocks.text:
`arr` has **automatic** storage duration: its lifetime begins when `intarray` runs and **ends when `intarray` returns**. `main` receives the address of memory that no longer belongs to any variable (a *dangling* address). Using it is undefined behaviour. On our machine gcc warns (`function returns address of local variable`) and the program crashes, but undefined behaviour has no guaranteed result: it could also print garbage, or even print what you hoped for, by luck.

**Rule:** never let an address of a local variable outlive the function call. If an object must survive after the function returns, it needs **static** or **allocated** storage duration. Day 18 shows the allocated way (`malloc`), which is how a function can really create and hand back an array.

blocks.q: Would it help to write `return arr;` as the last line instead of right after the declaration?
blocks.a: No. Wherever the `return` is, `arr`'s lifetime ends when the function returns, so the caller always gets a dangling address.

blocks.text:
### How to trace a scope and lifetime program

Exam questions give a short program and ask *what does it print?* A reliable method:

1. List the **globals** with their starting values (0 if none is given).
2. List each function's **static locals** with their starting values. These are set once, not on every call.
3. Go through `main` statement by statement. On each call, create the function's parameters and ordinary locals fresh; cross them out when it returns.
4. For every use of a name, find the **nearest** declaration above it (inner block first, then outer blocks, then file scope).
5. Keep a table: one column per variable, one row per step.

Try it on this program before you look at the output:

blocks.caption: trace.c

blocks.text:
| Step | global `total` | `calls` (static) | `main`'s `total` | printed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | 0 | 0 | not yet | |
| `int total = 100;` | 0 | 0 | 100 | |
| `add(5)` | 5 | 1 | 100 | `call 1: x = 5, total = 5` |
| `add(total)` passes 100 | 105 | 2 | 100 | `call 2: x = 100, total = 105` |
| final `printf` | 105 | 2 | 100 | `main: total = 100, c = 2` |

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o trace trace.c
$ ./trace
call 1: x = 5, total = 5
call 2: x = 100, total = 105
main: total = 100, c = 2

blocks.text: The traps here: inside `add`, `total` means the **global** (there is no local `total` in `add`, and `main`'s `total` is out of scope there). In `main`, `total` means `main`'s own 100. And `calls` counts across calls because it is `static`.

Make `calls` an ordinary local (delete the word `static`) and predict the output before you run it. Then put `static` back and instead delete `int` from `int total = 100;` in `main`, so it becomes an assignment to the global. Predict, compile, run.

### Key points

- An automatic variable dies when its function returns; an address of it is **dangling**, and using it is undefined behaviour. gcc warns: `function returns address of local variable`.
- An object that must outlive the call needs static or allocated (Day 18) storage duration.
- Tracing: globals and static locals start once (0 by default); ordinary locals restart on every call or iteration.
- Each use of a name refers to the nearest declaration in scope: inner block, then outer blocks, then the file.
- Keep a table of every variable's value; cross out locals when their block ends.

flashcards.front: What is the **scope** of a name?
flashcards.back: The region of the program text where the name can be used.

flashcards.front: Where does a file scope (global) variable's scope start and end?
flashcards.back: From the line where it is declared to the end of the file. A function above that line cannot use it.

flashcards.front: Where does a block scope (local) variable's scope start and end?
flashcards.back: From its declaration to the closing `}` of the block it is declared in. Parameters have the function body as their block.

flashcards.front: `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { ... }` then `printf("%d", i);` after the loop. What happens?
flashcards.back: Compile error: `'i' undeclared`. The loop's `i` exists only inside the loop.

flashcards.front: What does it mean that an inner declaration **hides** (shadows) an outer one?
flashcards.back: Inside the inner block the name refers to the inner variable; the outer one with the same name cannot be reached there. When the inner block ends, the outer one is visible again. They are different variables.

flashcards.front: Which gcc flag warns about hiding (shadowing)?
Why is `void g(int a[n], int n);` an error?
flashcards.back: Parameters in a prototype have function prototype scope and start at their own declaration, so `n` is used before it is in scope. Write `void g(int n, int a[n]);`.

flashcards.front: What is the **lifetime** of a variable?
flashcards.back: The part of the program's run during which the variable exists and holds a value. It is set by the storage duration.

flashcards.front: When is an automatic (ordinary local) variable created and destroyed?
flashcards.back: Created when its block is entered, destroyed when the block is left by any means. A function's locals are new on every call; a loop body's are new on every iteration.

flashcards.front: What is the value of `int n;` declared inside a function, before you assign it?
flashcards.back: Indeterminate (garbage). Reading it is a bug, and the output cannot be predicted.

flashcards.front: Which variables have static storage duration?
flashcards.back: All file scope (global) variables, and every variable declared with `static` (also inside a function).

flashcards.front: Starting value of a global or `static` variable with no initializer?
flashcards.back: Zero: `0` for integers, `0.0` for `double`, a null pointer for pointers. It is set once, before `main` runs.

flashcards.front: How does `static int s = 0;` inside a function behave?
flashcards.back: There is one `s` for the whole run, set to 0 once. It keeps its value between calls. Only that function can use the name `s`.

flashcards.front: Does `static` on a local variable change its scope or its lifetime?
flashcards.back: Its lifetime (the whole run). The scope is still the function's block.

flashcards.front: What does `static` on a file scope variable or function do?
flashcards.back: Gives it internal linkage: visible only in that one source file (like `private static` in Java). Its lifetime was already the whole run.

flashcards.front: Why is `static int v = start;` (with `start` a parameter) a compile error?
flashcards.back: A static variable is initialized before the program runs, so its initializer must be a constant: `error: initializer element is not constant`.

flashcards.front: Why is it wrong for a function to `return arr;` where `arr` is its own local array?
flashcards.back: `arr` has automatic storage duration; its lifetime ends when the function returns. The caller gets a dangling address, and using it is undefined behaviour (gcc warns `function returns address of local variable`).

flashcards.front: An object must still exist after the function that made it returns. What storage duration can it have?
flashcards.back: Static (decided at compile time) or allocated (`malloc`, Day 18). Not automatic.

quiz.explain: The inner block has its own `n` (7), which becomes 8 and is printed. When the block ends, that `n` is gone; `main`'s `n` is still 5, and `5 * 2` is 10.
The loop's `i` hides `main`'s `i` only inside the loop. After the loop, `i` is `main`'s `i`, which was never changed: 9.

quiz.answer:
f: v = 11
g: v = 11
f: v = 12
main: v = 11
quiz.explain: In `f`, the parameter `v` hides the global, so `f` changes only its copy: 10 + 1 = 11, then later 11 + 1 = 12. `g` has no local `v`, so it changes the **global**: 10 to 11. `main` prints the global, 11.

The global `count` starts at 0 (static storage). `bump` always uses the global: 2, then 4. `main`'s own `count` (50), declared after the first call, hides the global in the rest of `main`, so the last line prints 50.
`value` is a static local set to 5 once. `tick(0)` returns 5; `tick(2)` makes it 7; `tick(3)` makes it 10; `tick(0)` returns the remembered 10.
`a` is automatic: a new `a` = 1 on every iteration, so it always prints 2. `b` is static: one `b`, set to 1 once, doubled each time: 2, 4, 8.
`total` is a static file scope variable that `add_up` never resets. 1+2+3 = 6, then 6 + 6 = 12, then 12 + 1 = 13. This is the notebook's `sum_of2_fails.c` bug.
There is only one `id` (static local of `next_id`), shared by every call no matter who calls it: 101, 102, 103.

quiz.answer:
twice call 1
twice call 2
a = 6, b = 12, calls = 1
quiz.explain: Inside `twice`, the static local `calls` hides the global `calls`; it counts 1, 2. `main` uses the global `calls`, which starts at 0 and is incremented once: 1. `a` = 6, `b` = `twice(6)` = 12.

quiz.q: Which variable does NOT have static storage duration?
options: `static int n;` declared inside a function
`static int n = 1;` declared outside every function
quiz.explain: A variable declared inside a block without `static` is automatic. File scope variables and anything declared `static` have static storage duration.

quiz.q: A file declares `void f(void) { k = k + 1; }` and then, below `f`, `int k;`. What happens when you compile it?
options: It compiles; `k` starts at 0 and `f` adds 1
It compiles with a warning; `k` is garbage
It compiles; `f` creates its own local `k`
quiz.explain: A file scope name is usable only from its declaration to the end of the file. `k` is declared after `f`, so it is not in scope inside `f`.

quiz.answer: `sq` is a local array with automatic storage duration. Its lifetime ends when `make_squares` returns, so the returned address points to memory that no longer belongs to any variable (a dangling address). Reading through it is undefined behaviour: it may crash, print garbage, or seem to work.
quiz.explain: gcc says `warning: function returns address of local variable`. The object would need static or allocated (`malloc`, Day 18) storage duration to outlive the call.

quiz.q: A student writes `int total;` inside a function and then adds numbers to it in a loop. The program prints the right answer on their laptop. Is the program correct? What would you change?
quiz.answer: No. `total` is automatic and not initialized, so its starting value is indeterminate; it happened to be 0 by luck and could be anything on another run or machine. Write `int total = 0;`.
quiz.explain: Only static-duration variables (globals and `static` ones) start at 0 automatically. This is the notebook's `sum_of.c` bug.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between scope and lifetime, using a `static` local variable as the example.
quiz.answer: Scope is where in the program text the name can be used; lifetime is when, during the run, the variable exists. A `static` local has block scope (only its function can use the name) but static lifetime (it exists, and keeps its value, for the whole run).
quiz.explain: That combination is exactly why static locals are useful: the value is remembered between calls but hidden from every other function.

write.prompt: Write a function `int next_even(void)` that returns 0 the first time it is called, 2 the second time, then 4, 6, and so on. It must not use a global variable. Write a `main` that calls it 4 times and prints each result on its own line.
write.explain:
The function must remember something between calls without a global, so it uses a **static local**. `static int next = 0;` is set to 0 once, before the program starts, not on every call. Each call saves the current value in an ordinary local `result`, moves `next` on by 2 for next time, and returns `result`. Output:

```
$ ./next_even
0
2
4
6
```

rubric.item: returns the current value and adds 2 for the next call (first call returns 0)
`main` calls it 4 times and prints each result with `\n`

pitfalls: Forgetting `static`: then `next` is a new 0 on every call and the function always returns 0.
Adding 2 before saving the value: the first call returns 2 instead of 0.

write.prompt: Complete `average_so_far` so that it returns the average of every value it has been given so far. With the `main` shown, the program prints 4.00, 3.00, 5.00 and 4.00 on separate lines. Do not use global variables.

rubric.item: returns `total / count` (a `double` divided by an `int` gives `double` division)

pitfalls: Leaving out `static`: every call would see total = x and count = 1, so it would just return x.
Making only one of the two variables `static`: both must survive between calls.

write.prompt:
Write a function `int change(int x)` that returns `x` minus the value passed to it on the **previous** call. On the very first call there is no previous value, so it returns 0. Use `static` local variables (no globals). Then write a `main` that converts each command line argument with `atoi` (from `<stdlib.h>`) and prints the number and its change on one line. Example:

```
$ ./change 2 5 11 9
2 0
5 3
11 6
9 -2
```

rubric.item: a `static` local remembers the previous value
the first call is detected (a `static` flag, or similar) and returns 0
updates the previous value to `x` on every call, after computing the difference
`main` loops over `argv[1]` to `argv[argc - 1]`, uses `atoi`, prints `x` and the change

pitfalls: Updating `previous = x` before computing `x - previous`: the change is always 0.
Using `previous == 0` to mean "first call": it breaks when an argument really is 0. Use a separate flag.
Writing `static int previous = x;`: a static initializer must be a constant (compile error).
